We also explicitly rejected the adjacent idea — "did the agent do what it said?" — because it checks a claim against a claim: the agent's sentence sets the scope of what counts as explained, so a confused agent widens its own permission, and "fix bug" makes everything unexplained. An LLM reviewer is complementary to Gate, not a substitute: it reads what changed, we report what nobody looked at.

hostileRemovals can't reach revert — isn't removal the most breaking change there is?
Yes. It is the sharpest limitation we have, and it is in the report rather than in a footnote.

Gate builds one snapshot, of HEAD. A removed symbol is by definition absent from it, so Resolve returns nothing and the entity is tiered unresolvable. Measured on this repository: 19 of 19 renames and 27 of 28 removals. The behaviour is at least honest — such entities force continue, never keep. It is disclosed rather than fixed because sem.ProviderSnapshotOptions has no ref parameter, so resolving against the base tree is not a small change. It is the first thing we would build next.

hostileYour own output isn't byte-identical run to run. Isn't a nondeterministic gate broken?
The decision reproduces. The report does not quite — and we can tell you the line number.

internal/sem/analyze.go:1250 iterates a Go map when reconciling renames, so change_type flips between added and renamed on a handful of entities. Measured over five consecutive runs: the verdict, the exit code, the entity count and every header count were identical every time; the risk section differed by one finding — 17 diff lines of 173. The fix is three lines, sort the deleted keys before the rename loop, but it lands in internal/sem, which this project's contributor rules place out of our scope. The intended next step is to offer it upstream. We found it by running Gate on ourselves, and we chose to disclose it rather than paper over it.

curveballHow do you know your tier mapping is calibrated correctly and not just tuned to your repo?
We measured it on three repositories in two languages with the same binary.

The mapping keys on the provider's resolution strings, not on our repo's shape. entire-graph (Go): 52.8% exact. gorilla/mux (Go): 57.0% exact. pallets/flask (Python): 48.8% exact. The same seven resolution strings appear in all three, in comparable proportions, and entry-point relations appear in all three. Saved in curveball-cross-repo-generality.txt. A provider that renames or adds a resolution method degrades to heuristic — the safe direction — but the mapping would want re-measuring, and we say that in the limitations.

curveballWhat exactly changed at noon, and what proves you didn't break what worked?
Three tiers carried end-to-end, entry-point detection, verify commands, scope filtering. Three named tests prove nothing regressed.

TestFullyResolvedRepositoryIsUnaffectedByTiering, TestEvidenceSectionIsAbsentWhenAnalysisIsComplete and TestACompleteAnalysisAddsNothingToTheReport — a fully resolved repository renders exactly as it did before, no markers, no evidence section. All 27 pre-curveball tests still pass; exactly one fixture gained an explicit DependentsTier: Confirmed and its assertion is unchanged. We did not delete or weaken a test to go green.

technicalWhat does the graph give you that git can't?
Everything that makes ranking possible. Git gives lines; the graph gives entities and the relations between them.

Concretely: the entity-level semantic diff (added / removed / renamed / signature-changed / body-changed), the reverse-dependency walk over 12 edge types at depth ≤ 2, coverage resolution via incoming edges whose source lives in a test file, entry-point registration edges, and the resolution/confidence metadata the whole tier system is built on. Delete the graph and Gate has nothing to report — it is the substrate, not an integration.

technicalWhy doesn't internal/gate import internal/sem?
Because that would pull in tree-sitter and CGO, and it would have cost us the curveball.

gate defines its own Symbol and Relation; the impure collect layer projects real records onto them. That is why the entire signal/verdict/render surface is testable in sub-second synthetic fixtures with no CGO, no git and no toolchain, and why adding an evidence source is an additive file rather than a rewrite. The two-hour curveball turnaround is the return on that decision — although note the flip side, which is worth admitting: the projection is exactly where we dropped the resolution metadata in the first place.

technicalHow is coverage resolved? Do you run the tests?
No. It is graph-derived: incoming dependency edges whose source symbol lives in a test file.

The design originally called for a per-entity SearchRepository probe, but at ~400 entities that costs minutes. The edge-based approach is cheaper and still agent-independent, but it misses a test that exercises code without a resolved edge — disclosed. Two other honest gaps: TESTS edges are unusable on this repo (9 of 11,397 symbols, measured), and a test that asserts nothing still counts as covered — UNASSERTED is designed, not built.

technicalPerformance — will this run on a big monorepo?
~23 s wall / 57 s CPU at --profile full on this repository, rebuilt every run because Gate reads the working tree.

Larger repos need the durable cache: warm it once with entire graph index --repo . --head --profile full before a batch of runs. And --profile full is not optional for Gate — a shallower profile weakens call resolution, which is the evidence the verdict rests on. We would rather be slow than confidently wrong.

scopeWhy did you drop two of the four signals?
Time, in a cut order written before the clock started — and the two we kept are the two the verdict rule cannot function without.

Dropping coverage would have made revert fire on every change with a dependent, because nothing would have a covering test. That is a false accusation produced by a missing input, which is the exact failure unusable exists to prevent. Companion gap (FILE_CHANGES_WITH) and clone drift (SIMILAR_TO) are additive files, and their edges are already loaded in collect — the signals are independent by construction, so this is a day of work, not a redesign.

scope
scopeWho is the user, and how does this ship?
A developer deciding whether an agent's checkpoint is safe to merge — and it ships as an exit code.

0 keep · 1 continue · 2 revert · 5 unusable. That makes it a pre-push hook (~5 lines of shell) or a CI step, without any of Gate's output needing to be parsed. The pre-push hook is designed and was cut for time — say so plainly if asked; the exit codes it needs already exist and are tested.

scopeWhat's yours versus upstream?
Everything above commit 3a2a715 on main.

Gate is a consumer of the entire graph provider. New: internal/gate/ entirely (index, risk, coverage, verdict, render, types, changeset, evidence + tests) and the gate subcommand in internal/cli/gate.go. We deliberately did not modify internal/sem — including the three-line determinism fix we found there, which the contributor rules place out of scope and which we intend to offer upstream instead.

processHow much of this did the AI write?
Substantial assistance, disclosed in the submission — and the most interesting finding came from refusing to trust its output.

Claude Code was used for implementation, test authoring, debugging and documentation. Every design decision, the verdict semantics and all commits were human-reviewed and authorised, and the work is recorded as Entire checkpoints on the branch. The DATA_FLOWS direction bug was caught by reading Gate's own output and not believing it. That is not incidental — it is the thesis: agent-authored changes need evidence a human can check without reading all of them.

technicalAre there entry points you still can't see?
Yes — registration-shaped entry points are covered, dispatch-shaped ones are not.

Route and tool registrations now resolve through HANDLES_ROUTE/HANDLES_TOOL, so a decorator-registered handler reports a floor instead of a confident zero. But a Go type reached through an interface — net/http invoking ServeHTTP via http.Handler — has no such edge, so it still reports zero. That is in the limitations list, unhedged.

technicalThe scope filters exclude docs and data files. Isn't that you deciding what matters?
Yes, and we say so: they are Gate's judgement, not the provider's.

Two hand-maintained lists in internal/gate/changeset.go. The capability report cannot substitute for them — Markdown, CSS, Vue and Svelte all advertise exactly [CONTAINS, DEFINES], so it cannot separate a Vue component that embeds JavaScript from a CHANGELOG. Both lists fail toward disclosure: an unrecognised language is treated as able to hide a caller. And every exclusion is counted and printed in the report's SCOPE line, so you can audit the judgement rather than take it.

closingWhat would you build next?
In order: base-tree resolution for removals, then UNASSERTED, then the two cut signals.

Removals first because it is the biggest correctness gap. UNASSERTED second because "a test that asserts nothing counts as covered" is the one way an agent could actually game the coverage signal. Then companion gap and clone drift, whose edges are already loaded. And --explain <n> to print the dependency chain — the shortest path from "trust the number" to "check the number yourself."
